opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the thing I want most is for AI to take the friction out of the stuff people already care about. Everybody has a long tail of things they're curious about or want to get better at, and most of the time the barrier isn't motivation, it's the overhead. You want to learn a bit of music theory, or plan a trip, or understand some medical result your doctor gave you, and the hard part is finding the right information, figuring out what applies to you, and then actually doing the tedious steps.

So the picture I have is something like a really capable, patient collaborator who knows your context. Not just answering a question, but saying, "Okay, given what you've told me about what you're trying to do, here's the plan, and I've already handled the boring parts." For everyday tasks, things like scheduling, paperwork, comparing options, filling out forms, I'd love for AI to just quietly take those off people's plates so they can spend their time on the parts they actually enjoy.

And then for interests, I think the exciting thing is that it can meet you where you are. If you're a beginner, it can be a tutor that never gets tired of your questions. If you're an expert, it can be a sparring partner that pushes your thinking. That kind of personalized help used to be available only to people who could afford a private tutor or an assistant, and I think AI can make it something everyone has. That's the version of this technology I find most motivating.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as a collaborator, tutor, and sparring partner, but does not distinguish expertise from social companionship.

r002.rationale: It says personalized help can be available to everyone, but does not mention young children or access to detailed hobby knowledge.

r003.rationale: It mentions helping people learn and improve, but does not say AI should help them become experts in their chosen pursuits.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Thanks for having me. The thing I keep coming back to is that most of what people actually want from AI isn't anything exotic. It's the stuff that eats up their week. Figuring out which insurance plan to pick, planning a trip for a family where everyone has different constraints, dealing with the pile of emails that each need a slightly different kind of attention. None of that is intellectually hard, but it takes real time and real judgment, and right now people either do it themselves or it just doesn't get done.

What I want is for AI to take on that work on your behalf. Not just answer a question when you ask it, but actually understand what you're trying to accomplish, go do the pieces, and come back to you when it genuinely needs your input. The shift from a tool you operate to something more like a capable assistant who knows your context.

And the interesting part is that this is mostly a reliability problem now, not a capability problem. The models can do most of these individual steps. What they haven't been able to do consistently is string together ten or twenty steps without something going sideways, and then recover gracefully when it does. That's where a lot of the frontier work is, and I think that's what unlocks the everyday version of this rather than the demo version.

The outcome I care about is pretty simple. People get back hours of their week, and the things that used to fall through the cracks because nobody had time for them actually get handled. That sounds modest compared to the big narratives about AI, but I think it's the thing that will matter most to most people.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI as a capable assistant for everyday tasks, but does not distinguish expertise from social companionship.

r002.rationale: It gives examples such as insurance, trip planning, and email, but says nothing about hobby knowledge or young children.

r003.rationale: The response says AI should handle everyday work on people's behalf; it does not say AI should help people become experts in pursuits they choose.

astra-6.text: I want AI to help people do the things they care about. Sometimes that means taking care of an everyday task that feels like a chore, and sometimes it means helping you go deeper into something you love—learning a subject, making something, or exploring an idea. The goal is to give people more time and more ability to pursue their own interests.
